FAST

ZURICH, Oct 15 : Gianni Infantino apologised to the FIFA Council on Thursday, but English and German football chiefs said they remained unconvinced he was fit to continue as president of soccer's world governing body. Infantino said he had apologised during the closed meeting for mistakes in communicating and consulting over the now-abandoned FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) project, but stressed that it had been only a proposal and “in no way a done deal”. "First of all, I apologised for the mistakes that we made in relation to the communication and consultation process related to the FIFA Forward Enterprise project, which then led to many consequences," Infantino said in a video published by FIFA.  "But what is important to remember is that it was a proposal, so in no way a done deal."

The FFE plan involved creating a company to run the commercial interests of FIFA competitions, including the World Cup, and selling a minority stake to private investors. Infantino said it was intended to generate additional funding for FIFA’s 211 member associations. While Infantino appeared to retain strong support among African officials, opposition from some of Europe’s most influential football associations remained pronounced. German FA president Bernd Neuendorf called for a "complete restart" at FIFA, saying the governance reforms the organisation needed could not be delivered with Infantino in charge. "The first thing is we need reforms. That's true. And everyone knows that," Neuendorf said. "The old administration has to be reformed, and the whole governance has to be reformed. But I'm pretty clear here in this that this is not possible with Gianni. "So we need a complete restart, I think, a political restart." English FA chair Debbie Hewitt said Infantino needed to provide answers to questions raised by FIFA Council members and warned that failure to do so would make him unfit to remain president. "I think the man has to answer those questions," Hewitt said. "And if he doesn't answer those questions, no, he's not fit to be FIFA president." Neuendorf questioned the extent of Infantino’s apology, saying he believed it related primarily to the failure to consult the council rather than to the FFE project itself. "I didn't have the feeling that this apology was because of the FFE project in total," Neuendorf said. "My impression was it was just because it wasn't brought forward to the council and no one was involved." Neuendorf said council members had learned about the project through the media rather than from FIFA's leadership and that representatives from other confederations had also complained about the lack of consultation. "When it came to the FFE project as such, I have the impression that this still was not included when he apologised," he said. QUESTIONS UNANSWERED Hewitt said Infantino’s apparent regret over not consulting the council strengthened the case for releasing the relevant FFE documents to its members. "You have an obligation. We all have an obligation, a fiduciary responsibility to answer the questions that have been put forward," Hewitt said. "He told us to submit those questions. There were so many of them, and now it's up to him to do that and do that in the open way. "If there's nothing to hide, then share (the FFE documents) with us... if you regret it that deeply, please share it with us." The meeting also dealt with calls for reform at FIFA, but Hewitt said meaningful changes could not be made until members understood how the decisions at the centre of recent controversies had been reached. She cited FFE, the decision to suspend the automatic one-match ban imposed on United States forward Folarin Balogun after his World Cup red card, and the FIFA Peace Prize awarded to US President Donald Trump as issues requiring greater scrutiny. "Unless we understand what happened, either it was a massive failing in governance because it wasn't followed or actually the governance was followed, but there was something else that got to what we all felt in there was the wrong decisions," Hewitt said. "So we must understand what happened in order to be able to review it. Otherwise we're guessing." The criticism, however, was not unanimous. Ahmed Yahya, the president of the Football Federation of the Islamic Republic of Mauritania (FFRIM), defended Infantino, saying his leadership had helped develop football around the world, pointing to increased funding for national associations and the expansion of the World Cup to 48 teams. "We (the African nations) believe Gianni is the right person to continue leading football," Yahya said.  Asked whether most people wanted Infantino to remain president, he added: "I'm certain. The majority want Gianni to stay."

Source: Reuters

Oct 15 : Skydance's CNN said on Thursday it had agreed to a multi-year partnership with Google to explore how generative AI could help drive audience engagement across the network. The deal marks the first partnership announced since Skydance's merger with Paramount, under CEO David Ellison, who has sought to position the media group as a technology-driven business. As part of the deal, CNN will provide enhanced content rights for experimental features in Google's products. "Google's innovation with generative AI has changed how people discover information and content, and now those tools will help us explore new ways to discover and engage audiences," said Sam Felix, CNN's senior vice president of strategic partnerships and business development.

NEW YORK: The Nasdaq fell to near one-month lows on Thursday (Oct 15), weighed by a worsening selloff in AI-linked stocks on fears rising interest rates could impact artificial-intelligence investments, and fresh data pointing to building US price pressures. The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq marked their biggest one-day fall since July on Wednesday after hotter-than-expected consumer inflation data fuelled expectations of further interest- rate hikes from the US Federal Reserve, dragging on tech stocks. S emiconductor maker TSMC 's cautious note for 2027, citing macroeconomic uncert ai nties, also dented sentiment. Reports that AI lab Anthropic' s third-quarter revenue surged 45 per cent compared to the previous quarter failed to lift investor spirits.

Heavily indebted data-centre operator CoreWeave sitting in the eye of the recent tech storm, lost 8.5 per cent fol low ing a 15 per cent drop on Wednesday , while c loud computing giant Oracle was down marginally after a near ly 9 per cent fall in the previous session. The companies' bonds also fell, pushing their yields to record highs. Chipmakers lost ground, with Nvidia down 3.3 per cent, and Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices losing 5 per cent and 6.4 per cent, respectively. The broader chips index will have shed US$2 trillion in a more-than-14 per cent slide in seven sessions, if losses hold. It would mark its longest losing streak since May 2025. The S&P 500 information technology sector was the biggest drag, down 2 per cent. The slump pushed investors to government bonds, with the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield at a three-week low of 5.0725 per cent. " Investors are increasingly questioning how much future growth is already priced into valuations, how expansion is being financed and when these investments will generate sufficient returns," Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo, said in a note. "The repricing of CoreWeave's debt suggests that investors are becoming less willing to finance AI infrastructure growth at any cost."

Related:

Commentary: Every investment portfolio looks like the same trade - AI

At 9:50am ET (11:50pm, Singapore time), the Dow J one s Industrial Average rose 163.58 points, or 0.32 per cent, to 51,785.06, the S&P 500 shed 32 .20 points, or 0.42 per cent, to 7,686.74, and the Nasdaq Composite .IXIC lost 283.07 points, or 1.06 per cent, to 26,409.80. The CBOE Volatility Index, known as Wall Street's fear gauge, hit a two-week high and was last up 0.83 points at 17.74. Investors continued to segue into traditionally defensive sectors, with healthcare .SPXHC and consumer staples .SPLRCS rising more than 2 per cent each. Gains in these stocks propped up the Dow. The Nasdaq has dropped more than 4 per cent from record highs touched last week, with concerns about higher borrowing costs and AI spending threatening to eclipse the third-quarter earnings season, when S&P 500 profits are expected to grow 30.6 per cent, according to LSEG data. Data showed US producer prices increased by the most in 4-1/2 years in September amid rising goods and services costs, the latest indication of inflation broadening out beyond energy products. Markets will now scrutinize Fed Ch ai r Kevin Warsh's speech before the International M one tary Fund Annual Meeting. Shares of Rocket Lab dropped 1 5 per cent after the space company s ai d the inaugural launch of its new, larger Neutron rocket was delayed until next year. FMC slid over 38 per cent after the agrichemicals company sharply cut its third-quarter outlook, which includes a US$625 million-US$675 million hit from commercial actions. Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.78-to-1 ratio on the NYSE and by a 1.05-to-1 ratio on the Nasdaq. The S&P 500 posted 20 new 52-week highs and no new lows, while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 29 new highs and 261 new lows.

Source: Reuters/fs

BERLIN, Oct 15 : Germany plans a wide-ranging cooperation agreement with US chip maker Nvidia to boost the take-up of artificial intelligence in German industry, business daily Handelsblatt said on Thursday, citing people familiar with the issue. It said the deal would be announced next week at the Invest in Germany conference in Berlin, where Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang will be a guest. The aim of the deal would be two-fold, the newspaper said. Firstly, it would create the basis for physical AI tools, used in training robots or self-driving vehicles. Secondly, it would help to create high-performance AI models for industry. The newspaper said the agreement would involve investments in the hundreds of millions of euros.

WASHINGTON, Oct 15 : Nvidia and Apple each committed $25 million for US President Donald Trump's planned White House ballroom, according to a Washington Post report on Thursday that showed $333 million in private donations for the project. The Adelson family, longtime financial supporters of Trump and his Republican Party, committed $25 million as well, as did billionaire Charles Ergen, co-founder and chairman of telecommunications company Dish Network, the report added.  The president himself is not on the list, according to the Post. Reuters has not verified the report. The White House said it would not release information about the donors, which spokesman Davis Ingle said "represent a wide array of great American companies."

"The same critics who are alleging fake conflicts of interests, would also complain if American taxpayers were footing the bill for these long-overdue renovations," Ingle told Reuters. Nvidia said it was proud to make a donation to a nonpartisan trust that serves Americans. "As an American company, our support for the United States is paramount, and independent of any business interests," a spokesperson said. Apple declined to comment. The scale of the ballroom project and the administration’s handling of fundraising and disclosures have drawn criticism from watchdog groups and legal experts, who say it raises questions about transparency, donor influence and adherence to longstanding ethics and oversight norms. Trump initially said he and wealthy donors would pay for the estimated $400 million project, but he later unsuccessfully sought $1 billion from Congress for an underground bunker and security features to harden the facility. The Post reported that the "vast majority of the funds raised came from companies and wealthy individuals with interests before the federal government" and that half the total came from companies or executives of firms that have had federal government contracts in Trump's second White House term. The planned ballroom is among several projects Trump is pursuing in his efforts to remake Washington with sweeping, unilateral changes that his opponents have challenged in court and called a power grab. The US Supreme Court, in a 5-4 ruling in August, allowed Trump to continue construction of the ballroom while he challenges a judicial order that would halt much of the development. In a dissent, Chief Justice John Roberts said the project was "likely unlawful." The ballroom, which Trump has said will seat 1,000 guests, has faced public backlash. Preservationists and opponents say Trump exceeded his authority by demolishing the historic East Wing, which housed the first lady's offices and the White House movie theater, to make room for the structure. Trump says a planned 90,000-square-foot (8,360-square-meter) White House ballroom will include bomb shelters, medical facilities, defenses against drones and missiles and other security features. Confronted with criticism of the project, his administration now says the facility is needed for national security, an argument the president has also made about a proposed triumphal arch.

Source: Reuters

FAST

Oct 15 : The bones of a Neanderthal from a cave in Iraq's Kurdistan region are offering evidence of both violence and compassion in the closest evolutionary cousins of our species, exhibiting a wound apparently from a fatal spear attack as well as signs of an earlier nonfatal injury that may have elicited kindly care. Researchers have discovered at Shanidar Cave in the Zagros Mountains of northern Iraq a partial skeleton of a Neanderthal, aged in the mid-40s, that included a left shoulder blade, or scapula, with a circular hole six-tenths of an inch (15 mm) wide indicative of a deeply penetrating stab. The bones of this individual, who they call Shanidar A, were unearthed from under about 25 feet (7.5 meters) of rocks and sediment inside the cave and date to about 75,000 years ago. The researchers were unable to determine Shanidar A's sex. The researchers said the injury's shape suggests it was caused by a forceful thrust using a sharpened wooden spear, a type of weapon Neanderthals are known to have used, rather than a spear with a stone tip. It was a weapon employed in hunting large mammals that were an important food source.

"The spear would have gone through the skin and major muscles, especially the pectoralis, as well as the ribcage and muscles between the ribs, and the lung," said biological anthropologist Emma Pomeroy of the University of Cambridge in England, lead author of the study published on Thursday in the journal Scientific Reports. "The location could be like the kind of 'heart shot' hunters use to kill animals quickly by puncturing the heart, but that is a bit speculative. We do see heart shots as a hunting strategy both today and in the archaeological record. Neanderthals would have known this would lead to a quick death," Pomeroy said. University of Cambridge archaeologist and study co-author Graeme Barker, who has led Shanidar Cave excavations since 2015, said the likeliest scenario is interpersonal violence. The researchers said the violence probably occurred either between members of a particular Neanderthal group or between members of rival Neanderthal groups, calling a Homo sapiens attack or an accidental injury less likely. The researchers found shards of bone displaced by the weapon. The injury indicated that the spear entered from above with a downward trajectory, penetrating the left chest cavity from the front and traveling through the body before punching the hole in the scapula, causing quick death. ANOTHER INJURY In addition to the scapula, the researchers found some ribs, a nearly complete right hand and seven teeth, mostly from the front of the lower jaw, belonging to Shanidar A. The teeth bore evidence that this Neanderthal had survived brutal injury at least a year before death — a blow to the face resulting in front teeth being smashed and lost. One tooth was split, with half remaining rotated in the mouth and others pushed out of position. "The pain would have been extreme, and basic needs like eating and drinking would have been difficult, perhaps meaning Shanidar A needed food mashing and being able to rest. It's likely that Shanidar A did need some care from members of the group for some basic needs during recovery," Pomeroy said. Shanidar A was one of five Neanderthals, four adults and one infant, whose bodies were carefully tucked behind a rock pillar in the cave in a burial cluster within a generation or so of each other. The cave was occupied by Neanderthals for tens of thousands of years as a seasonal campsite, and later by Homo sapiens. Neanderthals were more robustly built than Homo sapiens, with larger brows. They lived as hunter-gatherers and inhabited Eurasia from the Atlantic coast to the Ural Mountains from about 400,000 years ago until a bit after 40,000 years ago, disappearing after Homo sapiens became established in the region. The two species interbred, with modern non-African human populations bearing residual Neanderthal DNA. The cave, overlooking the Great Zab river valley, has been a source of information about Neanderthals since the 1950s, with Shanidar A now offering new insight into their behavior. "We see evidence of two contrasting facets of human nature – care and violence – juxtaposed in the same individual," Pomeroy said. "We see evidence all around us today that violence and care are both aspects of how we humans behave, and we see this here in Shanidar A, too. Neanderthals were like us in many respects, both the good and the bad, and this find really highlights that, going against stereotypes of Neanderthals as unintelligent, uncaring cavemen and cavewomen," Pomeroy said.

Source: Reuters

WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump said on Thursday (Oct 15) the execution of the Fort Hood gunman would not be livestreamed but that immediate families of the victims would be able to view it in person. "I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device," Trump wrote. "He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed. That said, the execution may be viewed in person by the immediate families of the victims, if they so choose. They deserve to witness JUSTICE!" Some of Trump's fellow Republicans, including Vice President JD Vance, as well as religious leaders and international observers, had expressed doubts about the Pentagon's plan to livestream the Dec 3 execution of Nidal Hasan. Recent polls have also shown a majority of Americans opposed livestreaming it. Hasan, a former US Army psychiatrist, was found guilty in a military trial of fatally shooting 13 people at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009.

Oct 15 : Bodo/Glimt’s Aspmyra Stadium reinforced its reputation as one of European football’s most forbidding venues on Wednesday when Borussia Dortmund became its latest high-profile casualty, losing 1-0 in the Champions League. Situated above the Arctic Circle, the modest 8,270-capacity ground presents visiting teams with a distinctive combination of biting coastal winds, a slick artificial pitch and Bodo/Glimt’s relentless pressing game. The results speak for themselves. Since 2020, Bodo/Glimt have won 37 of their 48 European home matches, with AS Roma, Porto, Lazio, Manchester City, Inter Milan and Sporting among their victims at Aspmyra. "In windy, chilly conditions, the Norwegian opposition made more effective use of the ball on the artificial surface of Aspmyra Stadion," Dortmund's club website noted in its post-match summary, echoing a familiar sentiment from defeated visitors.

Bodo/Glimt midfielder Patrick Berg acknowledged the unique psychological edge their home ground provides. "We feel confident playing here at home. Many teams don't like to come here," he said after Wednesday's victory. THE ASPMYRA TRAP A string of upsets has earned the ground the nickname "The Aspmyra Trap". More than 800 kilometres north of Oslo, the stadium subjects visiting teams to sub-zero Arctic temperatures, biting gales and limited winter daylight. "To play football in Bodo in February, that is special for many teams and players, but we are used to it," manager Kjetil Knutsen has said. The stadium's synthetic pitch is engineered to withstand the harsh Nordic climate, but visiting players used to grass can struggle with the ball's unique bounce and speed, and the physical demands on the body. The home fans endure the elements to roar their team on at a draughty, outdated venue where only one corner of the stadium is fully sealed against the wind. SURFACE TENSION The surface has long been a point of contention for visiting managers. In 2022, then-Celtic boss Ange Postecoglou chose not to let his squad train on Aspmyra's surface the evening before their match, opting instead to complete their session in Glasgow. Celtic subsequently suffered a 2–0 defeat on the night, crashing out 5–1 on aggregate in their UEFA Europa Conference League tie. Former Roma manager Jose Mourinho, whose side suffered a 6–1 humiliation at Aspmyra in 2021, was among the pitch's most outspoken critics. "High-level football on a plastic pitch is not high-level football," Mourinho remarked. "The ball is slow and the players can't dribble... I don't understand why UEFA allows Champions League matches on a plastic pitch." Others regard the surface as integral to Bodo/Glimt's fast, aggressive style. "I love artificial turf. I love that style of football. It is tiki-taka, lightning-fast transitions, and a high tempo," Norwegian commentator Sverre Krogh Sundbo said. While the artificial pitch is likely to remain central to the club's identity, Aspmyra itself is nearing the end of its life. A new 10,000-seat stadium is under construction with fully enclosed stands, which should offer greater protection against the wind. Whether it will weaken the club's formidable home advantage remains to be seen.

LONDON, Oct 15 : Brazilian Rafael Camara will race for Haas next season on a multi-year deal, with the US-owned Formula One team saying on Thursday he was clearly the quickest in a shoot-out test for the seat. The 21-year-old Ferrari Academy driver leads the Formula Two standings with two rounds remaining, after winning the F3 title last year. He will be the second Brazilian on the starting grid, with Gabriel Bortoleto already racing for Audi, and plans to take the number 50 since his compatriot races with the 5 that would have been his first choice as a driver born on May 5, 2005. Camara replaces Frenchman Esteban Ocon, whose departure was announced last month, at the Ferrari-powered team. Britain's Oliver Bearman, who also came through the Ferrari Academy, is yet to be confirmed but sure to stay as the more experienced team leader.

The signing dashed the immediate hopes of Australian Jack Doohan, the reserve who had been hoping for a return to a full-time race seat after a split from Renault-owned Alpine last year. "He (Camara) was the quickest, very simple answer. He was impressive," Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu told reporters on a video call when asked what had decided the choice. RESERVE DOOR REMAINS OPEN FOR DOOHAN  Komatsu said Doohan's future with the team was "still up in the air" but the door remained open for him to continue in his current role. "We've been talking with him and his manager to see if we can do something together beyond this year," he added. Camara, a former teammate of Mercedes' 20-year-old Formula One championship leader Kimi Antonelli in the FRECA European junior series, showed his pace when he drove last year's Haas in a Testing of Previous Cars (TPC) outing in Portugal at the Algarve Circuit in August. "He showed... that he could handle himself very well with not a huge amount of time to learn the car, he showed us more than just raw speed," said Komatsu. "Rafa managed to create an environment to get the best out of himself, it was very impressive and certainly the laps he completed were special." The Recife-born Brazilian, who leads Red Bull-backed Bulgarian Nikola Tsolov by seven points in the F2 standings, said his first reaction when Komatsu called to say he had the job was to reply, "Are you sure?" "I'm extremely happy, especially for my parents," he told reporters. "It was a lot of sacrifice on their side. We are not even from the motorsports world, we didn't really know exactly what was the way to go and to be here. "We moved from Recife to Sao Paulo and then eventually they were always travelling with me. So their life, the normal life that they had, they couldn't be doing any more." Camara revealed that his grandmother had raced with a DKW Vemag in the 1960s, but said that was not the reason he had started. Instead the adventure began when the son of a work colleague of his father began karting and his brother then also got the chance but proved reluctant and eventually stopped. "I was always the one that was following and wanting to go but I was still too young, I was five," explained Camara, who has the late triple champion Ayrton Senna as his racing hero. "When I was six I kept asking my dad... and it became something a bit more serious now."   Haas are seventh of 11 teams ahead of next week's US Grand Prix in Austin, Texas. Bearman has scored 23 of their 30 points.

Source: Reuters

BANGKOK, Oct 15 : Japan told its G20 counterparts that authorities must watch exchange-rate moves with a high sense of urgency, Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said on Thursday. The G20 finance leaders re-confirmed their commitment on currency policy, Katayama told reporters after attending the group's gathering, held on the sidelines of the annual IMF meetings in Bangkok this week. "I told the gathering that we must closely watch financial market developments with a high sense of urgency," Katayama said on Japan's exchange-rate policy. The remarks came as the yen's persistent weakness keeps market players on alert over the chance of another round of intervention by authorities to prop up the currency.

BANGKOK, Oct 15 : The United States wants its global partners to rename artificial intelligence as "super intelligence," convinced that the new moniker better reflects the emerging technology, a top US Treasury official told Reuters in an interview on Thursday. Treasury Undersecretary for International Affairs Erin Browne said Washington was in negotiations with other shareholders of the International Monetary Fund about using the new term in a statement being drafted by the fund's steering committee, the International Monetary and Financial Committee. US President Donald Trump last month directed US government agencies to use the words "super intelligence" instead of "artificial intelligence" when referring to the technology. Browne said the United States, which holds the rotating presidency of the Group of 20 major economies, wanted the change to take hold internationally as well.

MANCHESTER, England, Oct 15 : Manchester City will attempt to keep their perfect Premier League start rolling at home to Ipswich Town on Saturday, with uncertainty over their punishment for financial rule breaches continuing to hang over the leaders. Enzo Maresca's City have won their opening six league games and sit three points clear of Arsenal, making a fine start on the pitch while their future off it remains unresolved. An independent commission found City guilty of 114 of the 115 charges brought by the Premier League. City have denied wrongdoing and lodged an appeal. The extraordinary backdrop has done little to derail City's domestic campaign. They underlined their strength with a 3-0 victory at 10-man Liverpool last Sunday.

The did lose 4-2 at home to holders Paris St Germain in the Champions League on Wednesday but return to the Etihad Stadium to face an Ipswich side sitting 10th on nine points. Former Manchester United defender Gary Neville said the uncertainty over City's eventual punishment had created wider frustration around the league, with the club continuing to win while the significance of those victories, with potential sanctions still to come, remained unclear. "This is not good for the Premier League, this is really bad for the Premier League — it's going to continue for a few months," Neville said on Sky Sports. "Up and down the country, (there's) a lot of annoyance that they see this team win football matches; it's just not going to be enjoyed." For champions Arsenal, who demolished Lille 3-0 in the Champions League on Tuesday, there is little room to surrender points if they are to keep pace in the title race. The London side sit second on 15 points and visit Nottingham Forest on Sunday knowing any slip could allow City to open a significant early gap. Forest are 15th with five points. SPECTACULAR LIVERPOOL VICTORY Liverpool will arrive at Brentford on Saturday with a different kind of momentum after a spectacular 6-3 Champions League victory at LASK on Wednesday. The night in Austria belonged to Bradley Barcola, whose hat-trick represented his first goals for Liverpool after going scoreless in his opening six appearances for the club. The French forward, whose frustrating start with the Reds had drawn increasing scrutiny, struck twice before halftime and completed his treble after the break as Liverpool made it two wins from two in the Champions League. It was a badly needed breakthrough for 24-year-old Barcola and a welcome response from Liverpool after their humbling home defeat by City four days earlier. Liverpool have been far less convincing domestically, however. They are ninth on nine points and face a Brentford side sitting a point above them in fourth, meaning Saturday could provide a sterner examination of whether the Reds' nine-goal European thriller has genuinely shifted their momentum. Manchester United's problems are more acute as they make the short trip to Elland Road to face Leeds United on Sunday desperate to breathe life into a troubled campaign. Michael Carrick's side have collected six points from their opening six games and sit 13th, already 12 points behind City after their worst start in 40 years. United slumped to a 2-0 defeat at Atletico Madrid in the Champions League on Tuesday and their latest assignment carries an additional edge against old rivals Leeds, who have made the stronger start and sit seventh with nine points. Three teams are still searching for their first victory, including bottom side Fulham who welcome Hull City on Saturday, Bournemouth who host Sunderland on Sunday and Tottenham Hotspur who are at home to Coventry City on Monday. With Manchester City trying to shut out the noise around their financial case, Arsenal determined to stay on their heels and Liverpool and United searching for a revival, the weekend should help show how the traditional heavyweights are coping.

Source: Reuters
